source_refs.note: Exercise 11.1, Question 1: book page 290 (Q1-Q8). The book prints no answers for Unit 11; every answer here is ours.

blocks.prompt: 1. Give two real-life examples where vector-valued functions are necessary.
blocks.explanation:
A theory question: we must name two real situations where one number is not enough and a vector function is needed.
The test: the quantity has two or three coordinates (a direction) that change with time.
Plan: for each situation choose axes, write \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) with \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}\) (and \(\hat{k}\)) components, and say why a single number fails.
steps:
Given: the definition of 11.1.2: a vector-valued function takes one input \(t\) and gives a vector output.
To find: two real-life situations that need such a function.
Method: look for moving objects whose position has several coordinates that change with time (like the book's projectile and drone examples) and build \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) for each with the three steps of 11.1.3: components, vector form, domain.

Example 1: a ball hit into the air (2D)
Origin at the batter, \(x\)-axis horizontal, \(y\)-axis vertical. Take horizontal speed 20 m/s, upward speed 15 m/s and \(g = 9.8\) m/s² (the model of the book's projectile example).
\[x(t) = 20t\]
\[y(t) = 15t - 4.9t^2\]
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = 20t\,\hat{i} + (15t - 4.9t^2)\,\hat{j}\]
Why: the ball moves forward and up or down at the same time, so its position needs two numbers at every instant; \(t \ge 0\) because \(t\) is time.

What the function tells us
\[\mathbf{r}(2) = 40\,\hat{i} + (30 - 19.6)\,\hat{j}\]
\[= 40\,\hat{i} + 10.4\,\hat{j}\]
Why: after 2 s the ball is 40 m away and 10.4 m high. A single number (say its distance from the batter) cannot tell both how far and how high the ball is.

Example 2: an aeroplane after take-off (3D)
Origin at the control tower, \(x\) east, \(y\) north, \(z\) up. Take ground speeds 200 m/s east and 150 m/s north, and a climb of 10 m/s.
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = 200t\,\hat{i} + 150t\,\hat{j}\]
\[\quad + 10t\,\hat{k}\]
\[\mathbf{r}(60) = 12000\,\hat{i} + 9000\,\hat{j}\]
\[\quad + 600\,\hat{k}\]
Why: after one minute the plane is 12 km east, 9 km north and 600 m high. Air traffic control needs all three coordinates at once; one number gives no direction.

More situations
The position of a satellite in orbit (the book's Figure 11.2), a drone on a search pattern, the GPS track of a car, the wind velocity at a weather station, the force on a robotic arm.
Why: each of these has a magnitude and a direction (several components) that change with time.

Check
Both functions take one input \(t\) and give a vector whose components are scalar functions of \(t\): exactly the definition in 11.1.2 \(\checkmark\).
blocks.final_answer:
(1) A ball hit into the air: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = 20t\,\hat{i} + (15t - 4.9t^2)\,\hat{j}\), \(t \ge 0\).
(2) An aeroplane climbing after take-off: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = 200t\,\hat{i} + 150t\,\hat{j} + 10t\,\hat{k}\), \(t \ge 0\).
In both, the position has several components and a direction, so a single number is not enough.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The textbook prints no answers for Exercise 11.1 (none for the whole of Unit 11). Every answer on this page is ours: worked out step by step, checked independently with a computer algebra system (sympy) and compared with a solution book. This question is open: many correct answers exist. Ours is one model answer built with the book's three steps (11.1.3); any function that models the motion correctly is also right.
